New machine. Its objects are: dudupe, risufek, livubir, bitevon, zuralo, zenafal.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to see how the machine responds.

TEST: dudupe, risufek, livubir
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three didn't light it, so I'll test the other three objects next.

TEST: bitevon, zuralo, zenafal
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Since the first group failed and the second lit up, the nexioms are most likely both among bitevon, zuralo and zenafal. I'll test one of them alone to learn whether a single nexiom is enough to light the machine.

TEST: bitevon
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Three facts so far: the first group (dudupe, risufek, livubir) did not light, the second group (bitevon, zuralo, zenafal) did, and bitevon alone did not. That points to two possible rules.

- **One nexiom is enough:** then no nexioms are in the first group, and bitevon is not one. Both nexioms would have to be zuralo and zenafal.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** then both are in the second group. The pair could be bitevon + zuralo, bitevon + zenafal, or zuralo + zenafal.

A third rule, "lights only with exactly one nexiom," is ruled out. If the second group held exactly one, the other would be in the first group, and that group would have lit.

Testing zuralo alone splits these cases:
- **If it lights**, a single nexiom is enough and the answer is zuralo + zenafal.
- **If it doesn't**, both are needed, and I have 2 tests left to separate the three possible pairs.

TEST: zuralo
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Here is what the four results tell me.

- **"One nexiom is enough" is ruled out.** Under that rule, the first group failing would clear dudupe, risufek and livubir. The single tests would clear bitevon and zuralo. Only zenafal would be left, but there are two nexioms.
- **"Exactly one nexiom lights it" is also ruled out.** If the second group held only one nexiom, the other would be in the first group, and that group would have lit.

So the rule is most likely that **both nexioms must be present**. That puts both in the second group. The possible pairs are bitevon + zuralo, bitevon + zenafal, or zuralo + zenafal.

Testing bitevon + zenafal:
- **If it lights**, the answer is bitevon + zenafal.
- **If it doesn't**, I'll use my last test on zuralo + zenafal to separate the remaining two pairs.

TEST: bitevon, zenafal
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

**The nexioms are bitevon and zenafal.** I've used five tests and don't need the last one.

The machine's response can only depend on how many nexioms are present: 0, 1 or 2. Checking each possible rule against the results leaves only one.

- **Lighting with no nexioms is ruled out.** Every such rule makes either bitevon alone or zuralo alone light up, at least one of which held no nexiom. Neither lit.
- **"Exactly one nexiom lights it" is ruled out.** If the second group held only one nexiom, the other would be in the first group, and that group would have lit.
- **"One or more nexioms lights it" is ruled out.** The first group and both single tests would clear five objects, leaving only zenafal for two nexioms.

The only rule left is that **both nexioms must be present**. Under that rule, bitevon + zenafal lighting up means both are nexioms. This also fits every earlier result: the second group contained both, and the first group and the single tests did not.

ANSWER: nexioms = bitevon, zenafal
One last question. If only bitevon were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. I already tested bitevon on its own (my third test) and the machine did not light up. That also fits the rule I worked out: the machine lights only when both nexioms are present. Bitevon is one nexiom, and alone it isn't enough.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: dizelin, bozagi, pusuni, bidefun, nifire, bemidis.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing objects one at a time to see how the machine responds.

TEST: dizelin
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine didn't light for dizelin alone. I don't yet know whether it needs one nexiom or both to light, so next I'll test a larger group of three to learn more per test.

TEST: bozagi, pusuni, bidefun
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Dizelin alone did not light, and neither did bozagi, pusuni and bidefun together. The rule could be "lights when any nexiom is present" or "lights only when both are present."

- **If any single nexiom lights it:** none of those four objects can be a nexiom. That leaves nifire and bemidis.
- **If it needs both:** the pair is not both inside {bozagi, pusuni, bidefun}.

Testing nifire and bemidis together works either way. If it lights, they are the answer under both rules. If it does not, the "any nexiom" rule is ruled out and I can narrow down the "needs both" case.

TEST: nifire, bemidis
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Dizelin alone did not light, the group of three did not light, and nifire with bemidis did. Under either simple rule ("any nexiom lights it" or "it needs both"), the nexioms would be nifire and bemidis. A rule like "exactly one nexiom lights it" is ruled out, because it contradicts the three results.

There is one more possibility. Only one of the nexioms might trigger the machine, with its partner sitting elsewhere. I have tests to spare, so I'll check nifire on its own.

TEST: nifire
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Dizelin alone, the group of three and nifire alone all failed to light, but nifire with bemidis lit up. If any single nexiom were enough to light the machine, nifire could not be a nexiom. Bemidis would then need a partner, but every other object has already failed. So the most likely rule is that both nexioms must be present, which makes the pair nifire and bemidis.

The one other possibility is that bemidis can light the machine on its own and nifire just came along for the ride. Testing bemidis alone settles this. If it does not light, both are needed and the answer is nifire and bemidis.

TEST: bemidis
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Here is what the tests show:
- Nifire alone did not light the machine, and neither did bemidis alone.
- Nifire and bemidis together lit it up.
- Dizelin alone and the group of bozagi, pusuni and bidefun did not light it.

So the machine needs both nexioms present at once. That makes the pair nifire and bemidis.

ANSWER: nexioms = nifire, bemidis
One last question. If only bemidis were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No, it would not light up. I already ran exactly this test, bemidis alone, and the machine did not light. That fits the rule the tests point to: it lights only when both nexioms, nifire and bemidis, are on it together.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: kolumes, bebula, ravonir, madenur, vuveku, ponala.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to narrow things down.

TEST: kolumes, bebula, ravonir
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three did not light it up. That could mean neither nexiom is in it, or the machine might need both nexioms present at once. Next I'll test the other three objects together to see whether they behave differently.

TEST: madenur, vuveku, ponala
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit the machine on its own. That suggests the machine may need both nexioms present together, with one nexiom in each half. If so, there are 9 possible pairs: one from {kolumes, bebula, ravonir} and one from {madenur, vuveku, ponala}. I'll test two objects from each side, which should split these possibilities about 4 to 5.

TEST: kolumes, bebula, madenur, vuveku
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit the machine, and four mixed objects didn't either. So the machine cannot simply light whenever any nexiom is present, because then one of the halves would have lit.

Two rules still fit the results:
- **Both nexioms needed.** The pair has one object from each half, but not one of kolumes/bebula with one of madenur/vuveku. That leaves 5 pairs: ravonir+madenur, ravonir+vuveku, ravonir+ponala, kolumes+ponala and bebula+ponala.
- **Lights with exactly one nexiom.** Both nexioms are in the same half, and test 3 had 0 or 2 of them. That leaves 2 pairs: kolumes+bebula and madenur+vuveku.

That makes 7 candidates with 3 tests left. Testing kolumes, ravonir and ponala splits them 3 to 4:
- **It lights** if the pair is ravonir+ponala, kolumes+ponala or kolumes+bebula.
- **It stays dark** if the pair is ravonir+madenur, ravonir+vuveku, bebula+ponala or madenur+vuveku.

TEST: kolumes, ravonir, ponala
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Three candidate pairs remain after the last result:
- **ravonir + ponala**, if both nexioms are needed.
- **kolumes + ponala**, if both nexioms are needed.
- **kolumes + bebula**, if the machine lights with exactly one nexiom.

A single yes/no test can't separate three options, so I'll use both remaining tests. Testing ravonir and ponala together should go like this:
- **It lights** only if the pair is ravonir + ponala.
- **It stays dark** if the pair is kolumes + ponala (only one nexiom present) or kolumes + bebula (no nexioms present). Then I'd test kolumes alone: it would light only for kolumes + bebula.

TEST: ravonir, ponala
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The machine lit for ravonir + ponala together, but ravonir alone (test 1) and ponala alone (test 2) stayed dark. That fits the rule that both nexioms must be present, with ravonir + ponala as the pair.

A few odd rules where one object switches the machine off would also fit every result so far:
- ravonir + bebula, lighting only when ravonir is present and bebula is absent.
- ponala + madenur, lighting only when ponala is present and madenur is absent.
- ponala + vuveku, lighting only when ponala is present and vuveku is absent.

I'll use the last test to check these. I'll put ravonir and ponala on together with bebula, madenur and vuveku:
- **It lights** only if the pair is ravonir + ponala.
- **It stays dark** under any of the odd rules.

TEST: ravonir, ponala, bebula, madenur, vuveku
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

The machine lit for ravonir and ponala together, but not for ravonir alone (test 1) or ponala alone (test 2). So the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it.

The last test ruled out the odd rules where one object switches the machine off. Adding bebula, madenur and vuveku to ravonir and ponala still lit the machine. Every result fits ravonir + ponala with the both-nexioms rule.

ANSWER: nexioms = ravonir, ponala
One last question. If only ponala were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. Test 2 was madenur, vuveku and ponala, and it stayed dark. Madenur and vuveku are not nexioms, and objects that aren't nexioms never affect the machine. So that test was effectively ponala on its own, and it did not light.

This also fits the rule the tests point to: the machine lights only when both nexioms, ravonir and ponala, are on it together.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: melikun, botabi, lepopol, kovukik, fogonan, pidudal.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: melikun, botabi, lepopol
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine stayed dark with melikun, botabi and lepopol, but I don't yet know its rule. It might light when any nexiom is present, or only when both are. Testing the other three together will tell me whether the nexioms are on that side.

TEST: kovukik, fogonan, pidudal
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit, so the machine cannot light whenever any single nexiom is present. One half would have to contain a nexiom. That leaves two main possibilities:
- **Needs both:** it lights only when both nexioms are on it, and they are split across the halves (9 possible pairs).
- **Exactly one:** it lights only with exactly one nexiom, and both nexioms are in the same half (6 possible pairs).

That is 15 candidate pairs to sort out with 4 tests, which is tight. Testing melikun, botabi, kovukik and fogonan would light for 8 candidates and stay dark for 7. That splits them almost in half.

TEST: melikun, botabi, kovukik, fogonan
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Three tests have all stayed dark, which leaves 7 candidate pairs under the two possible rules:
- **Needs both** (nexioms split across the two halves): melikun+pidudal, botabi+pidudal, lepopol+kovukik, lepopol+fogonan, lepopol+pidudal.
- **Exactly one** (both nexioms in the same half): melikun+botabi, kovukik+fogonan.

Testing melikun, lepopol and kovukik would light for 3 of these candidates (lepopol+kovukik, melikun+botabi, kovukik+fogonan). It would stay dark for the other 4. That split leaves both outcomes solvable with my remaining 2 tests.

TEST: melikun, lepopol, kovukik
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The last test lit up. Exactly three candidate pairs fit all four results:
- **Needs both:** lepopol + kovukik. Both nexioms were on the machine.
- **Exactly one:** melikun + botabi. Only melikun was on the machine.
- **Exactly one:** kovukik + fogonan. Only kovukik was on the machine.

Testing melikun alone separates these. It would light only for melikun + botabi under the exactly-one rule. If it stays dark, testing kovukik alone will separate the other two.

TEST: melikun
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Melikun alone stayed dark, which rules out melikun + botabi. Two candidate pairs are left:
- **Needs both:** lepopol + kovukik. Kovukik alone would leave the machine dark.
- **Exactly one:** kovukik + fogonan. Kovukik alone would light the machine.

Testing kovukik alone will tell these apart.

TEST: kovukik
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Kovukik alone stayed dark, which rules out kovukik + fogonan under the exactly-one rule. **Lepopol + kovukik** with the needs-both rule is the only symmetric candidate left, and it fits all six results:

| Test | Nexioms present | Result |
|---|---|---|
| melikun, botabi, lepopol | lepopol only | dark ✓ |
| kovukik, fogonan, pidudal | kovukik only | dark ✓ |
| melikun, botabi, kovukik, fogonan | kovukik only | dark ✓ |
| melikun, lepopol, kovukik | both | lit ✓ |
| melikun | none | dark ✓ |
| kovukik | kovukik only | dark ✓ |

One caveat: I assumed the machine treats both nexioms the same way. If it can treat them differently, one rule also fits every result: "lights when lepopol is present and botabi is absent." Under that rule the pair would be lepopol + botabi. Either way, lepopol is a nexiom. The symmetric needs-both rule is the simpler explanation, so I'm going with kovukik as the second nexiom.

ANSWER: nexioms = lepopol, kovukik
One last question. If only kovukik were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No. We tested this directly in the sixth test: kovukik alone did not light the machine. That fits the needs-both rule, where a single nexiom on its own never lights it up. It also fits the alternative "lepopol present and botabi absent" rule, since lepopol isn't on the machine. So the answer doesn't depend on which explanation is correct.

PROBE: no
